mainTopic: Does a משנה that names a neighbor's wall, storeroom, pit or plants prove that, where these are absent, one may place damaging things right at the boundary? The amud tests רבא's view against אביי.
overview: Before this amud, אביי and רבא argued about a field that is not set aside for pits. In the first version, רבא says one must still keep damaging things away from the boundary. The גמרא now brings one source after another that seems to say the distance is needed only when the neighbor already has something there. First come four cases that say to keep away 'from the wall': salt, lime and rocks; seeds, plowing and urine; a mill; and an oven. Each time the גמרא answers that the distance is needed even with no wall. The wall is mentioned only to teach what harms walls: these materials, dampness, shaking, and heat. The storeroom case is pushed aside because a home is different. The tree-near-a-field case is explained as fields with a rock underground between them. The tree-and-cistern case is answered by saying the cistern teaches how far roots spread, and a tree that 'came first' is explained as a case of a buyer. Last, the גמרא answers the flax-water, leeks and mustard case and then begins pressing on it using רבי יוסי's ruling about mustard and bees, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The משנה says 'from his neighbor's wall', so maybe no wall means no distance
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes quoting the משנה about keeping salt, lime and rocks three טפחים from a neighbor's wall. It infers that with no wall one may place them right at the boundary, which goes against רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: [One must distance] salt, lime and rocks three טפחים from his neighbor's wall, or else plaster the wall with lime. The reason is that there is a wall. So if there is no wall, he may place them right next to the boundary!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is reading the end of a משנה very closely. It is using the words 'from his neighbor's wall' to challenge רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה ties the three-טפחים distance to the wall. If the wall is the reason, then with no wall the distance should not be needed. That clashes with רבא, who says one must keep away from the boundary even when the field next door is not set up for pits.

keyTerms.meaning: Plasters (the wall) with lime to protect it
'The reason is that there is a wall; so if there is no wall…', a pattern for drawing a precise inference

steps.confusionAlert: This challenge is aimed at רבא's opinion from the earlier dispute, not at the משנה itself. The משנה is being used as evidence against him.

phrases.english: the salt, and the lime, and the rocks
phrases.notes: This picks up in the middle of a quote from the משנה, which opens with 'One must distance…'

phrases.english: three handbreadths from the wall of his fellow,
or he plasters [the wall] with lime.
The reason is that there is a wall,
but if there is no wall, he may place them close!

steps.triggerLanguage: טַעְמָא דְּאִיכָּא כּוֹתֶל, הָא לֵיכָּא כּוֹתֶל – סוֹמֵךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues an attempted challenge (begun just before this section) against רבא's view in the dispute with אביי.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's view (first version) that one may not place damaging things near the boundary of a field that is not set aside for pits.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's distance depends on there being a wall. So with no wall, placing these things near the boundary should be allowed.

steps.title: No, even without a wall you must keep away
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the inference. Even when there is no wall, one may not place these things near the boundary.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Even when there is no wall, he may not place them close.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back and says the inference is wrong. The rule to keep away applies with or without a wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The mention of the wall does not limit the rule. This protects רבא, because the משנה can now fit his view that one must always keep a distance from the boundary.

keyTerms.meaning: No. Here it opens a rejection of the proof.
Places close, brings right up to (the boundary)

phrases.english: No;

phrases.aramaic: כִּי לֵיכָּא כּוֹתֶל נָמֵי לָא סָמֵיךְ.
phrases.english: even when there is no wall, he also may not place them close.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא; כִּי לֵיכָּא כּוֹתֶל נָמֵי לָא סָמֵיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference drawn in step 1.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the inference from the word 'wall'. The משנה's rule itself stays.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It assumes the wall is a condition of the rule, when it may only be mentioned for another reason.

steps.title: Why mention the wall? These materials harm walls
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the mention of a wall adds, then answers: it teaches that salt, lime and rocks damage a wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what is the משנה teaching us? It is teaching that these things are harmful to a wall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the משנה mentions the wall at all if the wall doesn't matter. It answers that the wall is mentioned to teach that these substances damage walls.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After the rejection, the word 'wall' seemed useless, so the גמרא has to explain it. The answer gives the word a job: it tells us these materials are a danger to walls. It is not a condition of the distancing rule.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches us (what new point is being taught)

phrases.english: But rather, what does it teach us?
phrases.notes: In other words: if the wall doesn't change the law, why mention it?

phrases.english: This is what it teaches us:
that these are damaging to a wall.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֶלָּא מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן? הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the wall is mentioned, supporting the rejection in step 2.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the word 'wall' adds, if it does not limit the rule.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It teaches that these materials are damaging to walls.

steps.title: Second try: seeds, plowing and urine 'from the wall'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings another part of the משנה: seeds, a plow and urine must be kept three טפחים from the wall. Again it infers that with no wall one may come close, which goes against רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: one must keep seeds, plowing and urine three טפחים away from the wall. The reason is that there is a wall. So if there is no wall, he may come close!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the same kind of challenge with a different line of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This case also ties the distance to a wall. If the wall is the reason, then with no wall, sowing, plowing or pouring urine right at the boundary should be fine. That again goes against רבא.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One must distance the seeds, and the plow,
and urine
three handbreadths from the wall.
The reason is that there is a wall,
but if there is no wall, he may place them close!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: מַרְחִיקִים אֶת הַזְּרָעִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new attempt against רבא, built the same way as step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's view that one must keep away from the boundary even with no wall or pit next door.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The distance for seeds, plowing and urine is tied to the wall. So with no wall, coming close should be allowed.

steps.title: No, even without a wall you must keep away
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא again rejects the inference. Even with no wall, one must keep away from the boundary.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Even when there is no wall, he may not place them close.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the same rejection as before: the distance applies even without a wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as in step 2, the word 'wall' is not treated as a condition of the rule. That leaves רבא's view standing.

phrases.english: No;

phrases.aramaic: כִּי לֵיכָּא כּוֹתֶל נָמֵי לָא סָמֵיךְ.
phrases.english: even when there is no wall, he also may not place them close.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא; כִּי לֵיכָּא כּוֹתֶל נָמֵי לָא סָמֵיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference in step 4.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It treats the wall as a condition of the rule, when it is only mentioned for another reason.

steps.title: Why mention the wall? Dampness harms walls
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the wall is mentioned to teach that dampness damages a wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what is it teaching us? It is teaching that dampness is harmful to a wall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the wall is mentioned and answers that it teaches that moisture damages walls.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Seeds, plowing and urine all make the ground wet. The mention of the wall teaches that this wetness hurts a wall. It does not mean the distance applies only where there is a wall.

phrases.english: But rather, what does it teach us?
This is what it teaches us:
that dampness is damaging to a wall.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֶלָּא מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן? הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the wall is mentioned, supporting the rejection in step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the mention of the wall adds here.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It teaches that dampness damages walls.

steps.title: Third try: the mill kept away from the wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the משנה about a mill, which must be three טפחים from the wall measured from the lower stone, which is four from the upper stone. It infers that with no wall one could put the mill right at the boundary.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a mill must be three טפחים from the lower stone, which is four from the upper stone. The reason is that there is a wall. So if there is no wall, he may put it close!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes its third attempt against רבא, this time from the line about a mill.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The mill's distance is also measured from a wall. If the wall is the reason, then with no wall the mill could stand right at the boundary, which goes against רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: The lower millstone, which stays still

phrases.english: Come and hear:
and the mill: three [handbreadths] from the lower stone,
which are four from the upper stone.
phrases.notes: The bottom stone is wider than the top one, so three from the bottom ends up being four from the top.

phrases.english: The reason is that there is a wall,
but if there is no wall, he may place it close!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: וְאֶת הָרֵיחַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third attempt against רבא, built the same way as steps 1 and 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's view that one must keep away from the boundary even without a wall.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The mill's distance is measured from a wall. So with no wall, placing the mill close should be allowed.

steps.title: No, even without a wall you must keep away
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the inference a third time. Even with no wall, the mill must be kept away from the boundary.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Even when there is no wall, he may not place it close.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the same rejection as in steps 2 and 5.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once again, the mention of the wall does not limit the rule, so רבא's view still stands. The same answer works for all three cases.

keyTerms.meaning: He may not place it close (to the boundary)

phrases.english: No;

phrases.aramaic: כִּי לֵיכָּא כּוֹתֶל נָמֵי לָא סָמֵיךְ.
phrases.english: even when there is no wall, he also may not place it close.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא; כִּי לֵיכָּא כּוֹתֶל נָמֵי לָא סָמֵיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference in step 7.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It treats the wall as a condition of the rule, when it is only mentioned for another reason.

steps.title: Why mention the wall? A mill's shaking harms walls
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the wall is mentioned to teach that the vibrations of a mill damage a wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what is it teaching us? It is teaching that shaking is harmful to a wall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers why the wall is mentioned in the mill case: the shaking of the mill hurts walls. This closes the third 'wall' attempt against רבא, and a fourth (the oven) comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A turning mill shakes the ground, and that can weaken a nearby wall. Each of the three cases names a different way of harming a wall. None of them proves that one may come close where there is no wall.

keyTerms.meaning: Vibrations, the shaking caused by the turning mill

steps.whatToRemember: So far, every 'wall' challenge against רבא fails the same way. The משנה says 'wall' only to teach what harms walls (these materials, dampness, shaking), not to permit coming close where there is no wall.

phrases.english: But rather, what does it teach us?
This is what it teaches us:
that vibrations are damaging to a wall.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֶלָּא מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן? הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the wall is mentioned, supporting the rejection in step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the mention of the wall adds in the mill case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It teaches that the vibrations of a mill damage walls.

steps.title: The oven case seems to allow building at the boundary when there is no wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the משנה that a תנור must be kept three טפחים from the wall. It infers that with no wall, one could put the oven right at the boundary.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: an oven must be three טפחים from the wall, measured from its base, which is four from its upper rim. The reason is that there is a wall. So if there is no wall, he may place it right at the boundary!
steps.whatsHappening: This is the fourth try at the same proof. This time the גמרא uses the משנה about an oven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pattern is the same as with the dampness and the mill. The משנה requires distance only because a wall is there. So it seems that with no wall, there is nothing to protect, and he may build right next to the boundary.

keyTerms.meaning: The upper rim of the oven
He may place it close (right by the boundary)

phrases.english: Come and hear: and the oven —
three handbreadths from the base,
phrases.notes: An oven gets narrower toward the top, so three טפחים at the bottom works out to four at the rim.

phrases.english: which is four from the upper rim.
The reason is that there is a wall;
but if there is no wall, he may place it close!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: וְאֶת הַתַּנּוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the mill case was answered, the גמרא brings a fourth case with the same structure.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that one must keep away from the boundary even when the neighbor has nothing there yet.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה requires distance only because of the wall. That suggests that with no wall, no distance is needed.

steps.title: Even with no wall, the oven may not be placed at the boundary
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the inference. Even with no wall, one may not put the oven right at the boundary.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Even when there is no wall, he may not place it close.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the inference, just as it did in steps 5 and 8.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה mentioning a wall does not prove that the boundary is free when there is no wall. The rule to keep away stands either way.

phrases.english: No; even when there is no wall,
he also may not place it close.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא; כִּי לֵיכָּא כּוֹתֶל נָמֵי לָא סָמֵיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference drawn in step 10.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The inference from 'there is a wall' to 'with no wall it is allowed'.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The wall is mentioned for a different reason, not because the law depends on it.

steps.title: The wall is mentioned to teach that heat damages a wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה mentions a wall at all. It answers that the משנה is teaching that heat damages a wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then what does it teach us? It teaches us that heat is damaging to a wall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the wall is mentioned, now that it is not the reason for the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If you must keep away anyway, the wall must be there to teach something. The new information is that an oven's heat harms a wall. This matches the earlier lessons about dampness and the mill's shaking.
steps.whatToRemember: All four 'wall' cases (salt, lime and rocks; dampness; the mill's shaking; the oven's heat) get the same answer. The wall is mentioned to teach what damages walls, not to suggest the boundary is free when there is no wall.

phrases.english: Rather, what does it teach us?
This is what it teaches us:
that heat is damaging to a wall.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן? הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the משנה's wording after step 11 rejected the inference.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the משנה mentions a wall if it is not the reason for the rule.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: To teach that heat damages a wall.

steps.title: The storeroom case seems to allow a shop when there is no storeroom yet
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the משנה that one may not open a bakery, dye shop or cattle barn under a neighbor's storeroom. It infers that with no storeroom there yet, he may.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a person may not open a bakery or a dye shop under his friend's storeroom, and not a cattle barn either. The reason is that there is a storeroom. So if there is no storeroom, he may do it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a new kind of proof. Here, the neighbor's thing that needs protecting (a storeroom) is not there yet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה forbids the shop only because the storeroom already exists. That suggests that if the neighbor has nothing there yet, a person may use his own property freely. The same should then be true at the boundary.

phrases.english: Come and hear: a person may not open
a bakers' shop or a dyers' shop
beneath his friend's storeroom,
nor a cattle barn.
The reason is that there is a storeroom;
but if there is no storeroom, he may do it!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: לֹא יִפְתַּח אָדָם חֲנוּת שֶׁל נַחְתּוֹמִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another proof attempt. This one is about a neighbor's storeroom rather than a wall.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that one must keep away from the boundary even when the neighbor has nothing there yet.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ban depends on the storeroom already being there, so with no storeroom the activity is allowed. The boundary should work the same way.

steps.title: A home is a different case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that a דירה is different, so this case teaches nothing about other boundaries.
steps.simpleTranslation: A residence is different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes aside the storeroom proof by saying this case is special.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Using your own home is treated differently. If there is no storeroom yet, he may set up there. That does not prove a person may dig or build right at an open boundary.

phrases.english: A residence is different.
phrases.notes: The shop and barn here are inside the person's own home, under the neighbor's storeroom.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּירָה שָׁאנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case (a home is a special case)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The storeroom case shows that when the neighbor has nothing yet, any use is allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: That leniency belongs to a home in particular and does not apply to the general boundary rule.

steps.title: Support from the ברייתא: if the barn came first, it is allowed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports its answer with a ברייתא on that משנה: if the cattle barn was there before the storeroom, it is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The wording is exact too, as it is taught about it: if the cattle barn came before the storeroom, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds support for its answer by quoting a ברייתא taught about the same משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says outright that a barn already in the home is allowed if it came first. This is the home case the גמרא called special. So the leniency comes from the ברייתא's ruling about a home, not from a general rule that the boundary is free.

keyTerms.meaning: It is also precise (the text supports this)
It is taught about it (a ברייתא on that משנה)

phrases.english: It is also precise, as it is taught about it:
if the cattle barn
came before the storeroom, it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: דַּיְקָא נָמֵי, דְּתָנֵי עֲלַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up the answer of step 14.
steps.raayaObject: The answer that a residence is a special case.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא on the משנה: if the cattle barn came before the storeroom, it is permitted.

steps.title: Setting up a new proof from planting a tree near a field
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the משנה that a tree must be planted four אמות from a neighbor's field. It adds a ברייתא that the four אמות are for working the vineyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a person may not plant a tree near his neighbor's field unless he keeps it four אמות away. And it is taught about this: the four אמות they spoke of are for the work of the vineyard.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next proof. It quotes a משנה and a ברייתא here, and draws the inference in the next part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gives the reason for the four אמות: room is needed to work the vineyard, such as plowing next to the trees. This reason is what the next step will build on to argue about distancing from an open boundary.

keyTerms.meaning: The work of the vineyard (plowing and tending)

phrases.english: Come and hear: a person may not plant
a tree near the field,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן הִרְחִיק מִמֶּנּוּ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת.
phrases.english: unless he keeps it four cubits away from it.
And it is taught about it:

phrases.aramaic: אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת שֶׁאָמְרוּ – כְּדֵי עֲבוֹדַת הַכֶּרֶם.
phrases.english: the four cubits that they said are for the work of the vineyard.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: לֹא יִטַּע אָדָם אִילָן סָמוּךְ לַשָּׂדֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new proof attempt after the storeroom case was settled.
steps.kashyaTarget: The question of whether one must keep away from an empty boundary.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The setup is given here. The inference built on the reason for the distance (working the vineyard) comes in the next part.

steps.title: The vineyard reason suggests roots don't matter
steps.stepSummary: From the reason given for the four אמות (working the vineyard), the גמרא infers that a person could plant right at the boundary, even though roots damage the neighbor's field.
steps.simpleTranslation: The only reason for the distance is room to work the vineyard. So if that weren't an issue, he could plant close, even though the roots would cause damage!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now finishes the challenge it set up in step 16. It reads the reason in the ברייתא closely and finds a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the four אמות are needed for vineyard work, not because of roots. That suggests roots that spread into the neighbor's field are not a reason to keep away. This clashes with the idea that a person must keep his damaging things away from the boundary.

keyTerms.meaning: working the vineyard (room for plowing and tending)
may place close, here meaning planting right at the boundary

phrases.english: The reason is because of the work of the vineyard,

phrases.aramaic: הָא לָאו מִשּׁוּם כְּדֵי עֲבוֹדַת הַכֶּרֶם – סָמֵיךְ,
phrases.english: which implies that if not for the work of the vineyard, he may plant close,
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא from step 16, which said the four אמות are for working the vineyard.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּאִיכָּא שׇׁרָשִׁין דְּקָא מַזְּקִי!
phrases.english: even though there are roots that cause damage!

steps.triggerLanguage: טַעְמָא דְּמִשּׁוּם כְּדֵי עֲבוֹדַת הַכֶּרֶם, הָא לָאו מִשּׁוּם כְּדֵי עֲבוֹדַת הַכֶּרֶם – סָמֵיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge whose source was quoted in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that one must keep damaging things away from the boundary.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא gives only vineyard work as the reason for the distance. So damaging roots alone would seem to be allowed.

steps.title: A rock underground blocks the roots
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is talking about a case where a hard rock separates the two fields underground.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with? One where a hard rock separates the fields, so the roots can't get through.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the case. It says the ברייתא is about fields with a rock between them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a rock stops the roots, the roots can't damage anything. That is why vineyard work is the only reason left for the distance. So the ברייתא does not prove that damaging roots are allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: what case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a source to a specific case)

phrases.english: What case are we dealing with here?
Where a hard rock separates the fields.
phrases.notes: He means a rock under the ground between the fields, so the roots can't cross over.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 17.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא ignores roots, so roots that damage would be allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about a case where a rock blocks the roots, so there is no root damage to worry about.

steps.title: The fence clause supports the rock case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows the wording supports this: with a fence between them, each neighbor may plant right up to the fence.
steps.simpleTranslation: The wording fits this too, since it teaches: if there was a fence between them, each one may plant right up against the fence on his own side.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for its answer from a later line in the same source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both neighbors are allowed to plant right at the fence. That only makes sense if the roots can't cross, as in the rock case. So the source really is talking about fields with a rock between them.

phrases.english: The wording also shows this, for it teaches:
If there was a fence between them,
this one plants close to the fence on this side,
and that one plants close to the fence on that side.

steps.triggerLanguage: דַּיְקָא נָמֵי, דְּקָתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 18 from the wording.
steps.raayaObject: That the source is about a case where a rock blocks the roots.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The fence clause in the same source, which lets both neighbors plant up to the fence.

steps.title: Then how do roots reach the neighbor?
steps.stepSummary: The last clause talks about roots going into the neighbor's field. If a rock blocks them, how did they get there?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, look at the last part: if its roots went into the neighbor's field, he cuts them away three טְפָחִים deep so they won't block the plow. But if a rock separates the fields, what are the roots doing there?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the rock answer from the very next line of the same source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last clause plainly talks about roots that crossed into the neighbor's field. That can't happen if a rock blocks them. So it seems the source is not about a rock case after all.

keyTerms.meaning: digs down, cuts the roots away to a depth

phrases.english: If so, look at the last part:

phrases.aramaic: הָיוּ שׇׁרָשָׁיו יוֹצְאִין בְּתוֹךְ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ –
phrases.english: If its roots were going out into his neighbor's field,
he cuts them away three handbreadths deep,
phrases.notes: The neighbor whose field the roots entered is the one who cuts them.

phrases.english: so that they won't block the plow.
But if a rock separates the fields,
what are the roots doing there?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אֵימָא סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rock answer of step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the source is about a case where a rock blocks the roots.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The last clause has roots crossing into the neighbor's field, which a rock would prevent.

steps.title: The last clause is a separate no-rock case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the last clause is a new case: where there is no rock and the roots did cross over.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it means: and if there is no rock, and its roots went into the neighbor's field, he cuts them away three טְפָחִים deep so they won't block the plow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by reading the last clause as a separate case that does not have the rock.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first part of the source is about fields with a rock. The last part adds another case, where there is no rock. So the rock answer still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: this is what it means (rereading the source)

steps.whatToRemember: The four-אמות rule is read as a rock case, so it does not prove that roots may damage. Only the משנה's last clause, a separate case, deals with roots that crossed over.

phrases.english: This is what it means:
And if there is no rock,

phrases.aramaic: וְהָיוּ שׇׁרָשָׁיו יוֹצְאִין לְתוֹךְ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ –
phrases.english: and its roots were going out into his neighbor's field,
he cuts them away three handbreadths deep,
so that they won't block the plow.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the source as two separate cases
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The last clause shows the whole source is about a case with no rock.
steps.terutzMaskana: The last clause is its own case without a rock. The earlier part is still about a rock case.

steps.title: The tree and the בּוֹר: no בּוֹר means plant close?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the משנה that a tree must be twenty-five אמות from a בּוֹר. It infers that with no בּוֹר there, he could plant close.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: one must keep a tree twenty-five אמות away from a בּוֹר. The reason is that there is a בּוֹר. So if there is no בּוֹר, he may plant close!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new challenge from a different משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה requires distance only because a בּוֹר is there. That suggests that where the neighbor has nothing yet, a person may plant at the boundary. This challenges the view that he must keep away even before the neighbor has anything there.

keyTerms.meaning: cistern, a pit for storing water

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One must keep a tree away from a cistern
twenty-five cubits.
The reason is that there is a cistern,
which implies that if there is no cistern, he may plant close!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: מַרְחִיקִין אֶת הָאִילָן מִן הַבּוֹר עֶשְׂרִים וְחָמֵשׁ אַמָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new challenge of the same type as step 13, from a different משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that one must keep damaging things away from the boundary even when the neighbor has nothing there yet.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The distance depends on the בּוֹר being there. So with no בּוֹר, planting close would be allowed.

steps.title: The בּוֹר teaches how far roots spread
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that even without a בּוֹר he may not plant close. The משנה names the בּוֹר only to teach that roots spread up to twenty-five אמות and damage it.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Even when there is no בּוֹר, he may not plant close. The משנה is teaching us that roots travel up to twenty-five אמות and damage a בּוֹר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the inference. It explains why the משנה mentions a בּוֹר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The בּוֹר is not the condition for having to keep away. The משנה mentions it to tell us the distance: roots can reach and harm a בּוֹר up to twenty-five אמות away. This is like step 12, where the wall was mentioned to teach a fact about damage.

keyTerms.meaning: and this is what it teaches us

steps.whatToRemember: Mentioning a בּוֹר in the משנה does not mean planting close is allowed without one. It teaches how far roots can spread and cause damage.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read the 'reason is there is a בּוֹר' inference as the conclusion. The גמרא rejects it.

phrases.english: No;

phrases.aramaic: כִּי לֵיכָּא בּוֹר נָמֵי לָא סָמֵיךְ,
phrases.english: even when there is no cistern, he may not plant close,
and this is what it teaches us:
that up to twenty-five cubits,
roots travel and damage a cistern.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא; כִּי לֵיכָּא בּוֹר נָמֵי לָא סָמֵיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining why the case is mentioned (to teach a fact)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without a בּוֹר, planting close is allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Planting close is not allowed even without a בּוֹר. The בּוֹר is mentioned to teach that roots damage it up to twenty-five אמות away.

steps.title: If a tree may never be planted close, how can it come first?
steps.stepSummary: The last clause of the בּוֹר משנה says that if the tree came first, he does not cut it down. If a tree may never be planted close, how could that happen?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, look at the last clause: 'If the tree came first, he does not cut it down.' But if he is never allowed to plant close, how could you ever find such a case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 23 by quoting the end of the same משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 23 the גמרא said a tree may not be planted near the boundary even when no בּוֹר is there. But the משנה describes a tree that was there before the בּוֹר and was allowed to stay. If planting it close was never allowed, that tree should never have been there legally.

keyTerms.meaning: If so: if what you just said is true
Say the last clause: look at the end of the same משנה
He does not cut it down
How can you find such a case?

phrases.english: If so, say the last clause:
And if the tree came first, he does not cut it down.
But if he may not place it close,
how can you find such a case?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אֵימָא סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the תירוץ of step 23 using the end of the same משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 23 that a tree may never be planted close, even with no בּוֹר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The סיפא speaks of a legal tree that came before the בּוֹר. That case seems impossible if planting close is always forbidden.

steps.title: The tree came first in a case of a buyer
steps.stepSummary: Like רב פפא says elsewhere, the case is a buyer. Here too it is a buyer.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב פפא said, it is talking about a buyer. Here too, it is talking about a buyer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the case of a tree coming first happens when one person owned both the tree and the בּוֹר and then sold part of the field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When one owner had both in his own field, the tree near the בּוֹר broke no rule. Once he sold the part with the בּוֹר, the tree is already there and does not have to be cut down. So the סיפא is possible even if planting close is normally forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: Buyer: someone who bought part of the field
So too: the same applies here

steps.whatToRemember: A tree can 'come first' legally when one person owned both the tree and the בּוֹר and then sold one part to a buyer.

phrases.english: As רב פפא said: with a buyer;
phrases.notes: רב פפא gave this answer to a similar question somewhere else, and the גמרא borrows it here.

phrases.english: so too here, with a buyer.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּדְאָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: בְּלוֹקֵחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the סיפא is about a buyer.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A tree that came first must have been planted close with no בּוֹר there, which would mean planting close is allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The tree was planted when one owner had both. It became a neighbor's problem only after a sale, so planting close stays forbidden.

steps.title: A new משנה seems to allow placing close when nothing is there
steps.stepSummary: A משנה says to keep flax-water from vegetables, leeks from onions, and mustard from bees. The reason is that vegetables are there, so with no vegetables he could place it close.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: We keep flax-soaking water away from vegetables, leeks away from onions, and mustard away from bees. The reason is that there are vegetables. So if there are no vegetables, he may place it close!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new משנה to challenge its position that a damaging thing may not be placed close even when nothing is there to damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same kind of challenge as step 22, from a different משנה. The משנה names the thing being damaged, the vegetables. That seems to show that the rule only applies when vegetables are there.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
We distance the flax-soaking water from vegetables,
and the leeks from the onions,
and the mustard from the bees.
The reason is that there are vegetables,
but if there are no vegetables, he may place it close!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: מַרְחִיקִין אֶת הַמִּשְׁרָה מִן הַיָּרָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new source with the same kind of inference as step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: The position that a damaging thing may not be placed close even when nothing is there to damage.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה names the vegetables, which suggests that without vegetables there is no need to keep a distance.

steps.title: The משנה only teaches that these things harm each other
steps.stepSummary: No, even with no vegetables he may not place it close. The משנה is teaching that these items harm each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Even when there are no vegetables he may not place it close. The משנה teaches us that these things are harmful to each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the inference. The משנה names the vegetables only to tell us which things harm which.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This matches the answer in step 23. The משנה lists pairs to teach a fact we might not know, for example that leeks hurt onions. It is not saying the distance is needed only when the other item is already there.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches us: this is the new point
They are harmful to each other

steps.whatToRemember: When a משנה names the thing being damaged, it may only be teaching that the two things harm each other. It does not have to mean the rule applies only when that thing is present.

phrases.english: No; even when there are no vegetables
he also may not place it close;
and this is what it teaches us:
that these are harmful to each other.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא; כִּי לֵיכָּא יָרָק נָמֵי לָא סָמֵיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 26, the same way step 23 answered step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading why the משנה names each item.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The vegetables are named because the rule depends on them being there.
steps.terutzMaskana: The items are named to teach which things harm each other, and the distance is needed either way.

steps.title: Quoting רבי יוסי on mustard to challenge the answer
steps.stepSummary: If so, look at the last clause: רבי יוסי permits mustard, because the mustard owner can say: keep your bees away from my mustard, since they eat my mustard plants.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, look at the last clause: רבי יוסי permits mustard, because he can say to him: 'Before you tell me to keep my mustard away from your bees, keep your bees away from my mustard, because they come and eat my mustard blossoms.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the last clause of the same משנה to challenge the answer in step 27. This step sets up the challenge, and the גמרא will explain the difficulty in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי's argument is about bees that are already there and are eating the mustard right now. The גמרא is about to use this argument to test whether the distance rule really applies even when the neighbor's item is not there.

keyTerms.meaning: Before you tell me: you should first fix your own side
Blossoms or tender shoots of a plant

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יוסי does not say mustard and bees don't harm each other. He says each side harms the other, so the bee owner cannot demand that only the mustard be moved.

phrases.english: If so, say the last clause:
רבי יוסי permits it with mustard,
because he can say to him:
phrases.notes: The mustard owner is speaking to the bee owner.

phrases.english: Before you tell me,
'Keep your mustard away from my bees,'
keep your bees away from my mustard,
because they come and eat the blossoms of my mustard.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אֵימָא סֵיפָא: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי מַתִּיר בְּחַרְדָּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the תירוץ of step 27 using the end of the same משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 27 that the משנה only teaches which items harm each other, and that the distance applies even when the other item is absent.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוסי's argument assumes the bees are already there and causing harm. The גמרא will press this point in the next lines.
